name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,159

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Vagrant we like prints an alternative to Robinson Crusoe and Lemuel Gulliver

definitions.text: an alternative to Robinson Crusoe and Lemuel Gulliver

indicators.note: a vagrant wanders with no fixed home, so the letters that follow roam out of their order

blocks.note: the twelve letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A tramp who enjoys reading picks a different shipwreck story from Defoe's and Swift's.
explanation.walkthrough: PETER WILKINS is Robert Paltock's 1750 novel of a castaway who finds a race of flying people, a rival to Crusoe and Gulliver as a castaway fantasy.
explanation.definitionFit: Paltock's hero is another shipwrecked traveller in eighteenth-century fiction, so his book is an alternative read to Defoe and Swift.

clue.text: A wet alternative to BBC Alba or S4C?

definitions.text: A wet alternative to BBC Alba or S4C?

blocks.clueFragment: alternative to BBC Alba or S4C
blocks.note: surface reading: another television channel, like the Gaelic BBC Alba or the Welsh S4C
setter's reading: a body of water between two countries, named like a TV station in a third language

explanation.surface: Asking for a soggy rival to Britain's Gaelic and Welsh-language TV stations.
explanation.walkthrough: BBC Alba broadcasts in Scottish Gaelic and S4C in Welsh; the answer is the sea strait between England and France.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea strait off southern England shares its name pattern with a language-based TV station, but is made of water.

clue.text: The death we hear about in Under Milk Wood

definitions.text: The death we hear about in Under Milk Wood

blocks.note: surface reading: a death reported in the play
setter's reading: the undertaker in Dylan Thomas's play is nicknamed after his trade

explanation.surface: A demise that is mentioned in Dylan Thomas's radio play.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas's Welsh villagers are named by trade: the undertaker is Evans the Death.
explanation.definitionFit: In the play the undertaker's nickname is 'the Death', so the surname is the man bearing that label.

clue.text: Dwarves possibly seen by Toad and Badger

definitions.text: Dwarves possibly seen by Toad and Badger

blocks.note: surface reading: little people from fairy tale
setter's reading: dwarf varieties of the trees in the title of The Wind in the Willows

explanation.surface: Small folk who might have been spotted by the animals of a children's classic.
explanation.walkthrough: Toad and Badger live in Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows; there are dwarf species of willow.
explanation.definitionFit: Some willows are dwarf species, and riverbank willows are what Grahame's animals see around them.

clue.text: "I have forgotten everything I used to know so —" (Christina Rossetti)

definitions.text: "I have forgotten everything I used to know so —" (Christina Rossetti)

blocks.clueFragment: "I have forgotten everything I used to know so —"
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse with its final words left blank
setter's reading: complete the line by Rossetti with the phrase meaning in the distant past

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing words end Rossetti's line.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase meaning in the distant past completes the poet's line about having forgotten what she once knew.

clue.text: The problem found with fame and fortune

definitions.text: The problem found with fame and fortune

blocks.note: setter's reading: a trouble or harm
surface reading: the downside of celebrity, but really the word placed before each of these to form 'bad repute' and 'bad luck'

explanation.surface: The drawback that comes with being rich and famous.
explanation.walkthrough: The word precedes both 'fame' and 'fortune' to make the phrases for a bad reputation and bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word means a harm or trouble, and it pairs with fame and fortune as their negative prefix.

clue.text: The manuscript found in this Spanish city was written by a Pole

definitions.text: The manuscript found in this Spanish city was written by a Pole

blocks.clueFragment: The manuscript found in this Spanish city
blocks.note: surface reading: a document discovered in a Spanish town
setter's reading: Jan Potocki's novel takes its title from this city

explanation.surface: A paper discovered in a Spanish city turns out to be the work of a Polish writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Jan Potocki, a Polish count, wrote 'The Manuscript Found in Saragossa'; the city is now usually spelt Zaragoza.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aragonese city names the title of Potocki's frame-tale novel, so it is where his manuscript was found.

clue.text: All I need is dispensed by a wise man – the Last Puritan's uncle

indicators.note: a pharmacist dispenses by making things up, so these letters are made up anew

blocks.note: Lessing's play 'Nathan the Wise'
the eight letters of these words reordered

explanation.surface: Everything I require is handed out by a sage, the uncle of Santayana's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: The Last Puritan is George Santayana's novel; its hero Oliver Alden has an uncle of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Santayana's novel the title character, Oliver Alden, is nephew to this man, his father's brother.

clue.text: Site of major work in marble and silver, by a recognized artist

definitions.text: Site of major work in marble

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a Royal Academician, an artist given official recognition by the Royal Academy

explanation.surface: A sculptor's masterpiece in marble and silver stands somewhere, made by an acclaimed artist.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'major work in marble' is the Taj Mahal; RA after a British artist's name marks membership of the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian city is home to the Taj Mahal, the great white marble mausoleum, so it is that monument's location.

clue.text: Role no lady played in an inter-war tale of conspiracy

indicators.note: something played is performed in a new way, so the letters are acted out in a fresh order

blocks.note: all ten letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A part that no actress took in a plotting novel from between the wars.
explanation.walkthrough: LONELY ROAD is Nevil Shute's 1932 thriller about gun-running and a political plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Shute's novel came out between the two world wars and turns on a conspiracy, so it is such a tale by title.

clue.text: Result of 5 journeys by fictitious explorer around Italy, Austria, Sweden and Portugal

indicators.note: one thing placed around others encloses them, so the explorer wraps the country letters

blocks.note: Dora the Explorer, the cartoon heroine
international vehicle code for Italy
international vehicle code for Austria
international vehicle code for Sweden
international vehicle code for Portugal

explanation.surface: A make-believe explorer's travels round four European countries had a lasting outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: '5' points to 5-down, LONG AGO: journeys made long ago scattered a people. The country codes are those on car nationality stickers.
explanation.definitionFit: A diaspora is a people dispersed from its homeland, the outcome of migrations made in the distant past.

clue.text: I start to hunt in small measure, creating much resistance

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
these pieces go in the measure, enclosed by its two letters

blocks.note: mm, the abbreviation for millimetre, a small unit of length
ego is Latin for I, the self
opening letter of hunt

explanation.surface: I begin hunting on a modest scale and this stirs up great opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: The two letters of the millimetre symbol split to hold the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A megohm is a million ohms, a unit of electrical resistance, so it measures a great deal of it.

clue.text: It's clear Smike's moved a young lady in a Dickens novel

definitions.text: a young lady in a Dickens novel

indicators.note: things that have been moved are shifted about, so these letters change places

blocks.note: every letter of these two words

explanation.surface: Plainly Smike, of Nicholas Nickleby, has touched a girl in a Dickens story.
explanation.walkthrough: Smike is from Nicholas Nickleby, but the answer is the headmaster's daughter at Salem House in David Copperfield.
explanation.definitionFit: The daughter of Copperfield's brutal schoolmaster is a girl in that Dickens book, referred to by this title and surname.

clue.text: Jane's friends of a famous detective?

definitions.text: Jane's friends of a famous detective?

blocks.clueFragment: Jane's friends of a famous detective?
blocks.note: surface reading: some woman called Jane knows the relatives of Sherlock Holmes's companion
setter's reading: Jane Austen's unfinished novel, whose title family shares a name with Holmes's sidekick

explanation.surface: A woman named Jane is acquainted with the family of a celebrated sleuth.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Austen began a novel about a family of this name and abandoned it; Dr Watson is Sherlock Holmes's friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's fragment is titled after a family that shares its surname with Holmes's loyal companion, so it is literally that family.

clue.text: For Christopher Robin, a place not spoken about and unknown, but Hardy wrote of exploits there

blocks.clueFragment: For Christopher Robin, a place not spoken about
blocks.note: in Winnie-the-Pooh, Christopher Robin says there are East and West Poles but people don't like talking about them
y is a mathematical unknown; 'and' adds it on

explanation.surface: A spot Christopher Robin kept quiet about, an obscure place that Hardy nonetheless described.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hardy wrote a boys' story, 'Our Exploits at West Poley', set in a Somerset village.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's children's tale is titled for the adventures of two boys in this village, so he wrote of exploits there.

clue.text: The kind of music that was very influential in China 1000 years ago

definitions.text: very influential in China 1000 years ago

blocks.note: first meaning: a piece of music for singing

blocks.clueFragment: very influential in China 1000 years ago
blocks.note: second meaning: the dynasty that ruled China from 960 to 1279

explanation.surface: A style of music that held great sway in China a millennium ago.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an ordinary sung piece and the name of the imperial Chinese dynasty that ruled around the year 1000.

clue.text: What the prophet said, according to Nietzsche?

definitions.text: What the prophet said, according to Nietzsche?

blocks.note: surface reading: asking for the words a prophet spoke
setter's reading: the first word of the English title of Nietzsche's book about his Persian prophet

explanation.surface: A question about what Nietzsche reports a prophet saying.
explanation.walkthrough: Nietzsche's book is known in English as 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra', and Zarathustra is its prophet.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening word of the English title of Nietzsche's work introduces the prophet's speech, so it is literally what he 'said'.

clue.text: Austen's nice translation reads well

indicators.note: a translation renders words into another form, so the letters are rendered in a new order

blocks.note: the novelist's name; the 's links it to the translation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pleasant translation of Jane Austen is a good read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reads well' here means speaks aloud clearly, not makes a good book.
explanation.definitionFit: To enunciate is to pronounce words distinctly, which is what a person who reads well out loud does.

clue.text: Fur-lined gear for two Germans in their submarine

indicators.note: the two men are placed inside the vessel that belongs to them

blocks.note: the German word for a submarine, U-Boot
G is the abbreviation for German, twice

explanation.surface: Warm, sheepskin-lined kit for two German sailors aboard their U-boat.
explanation.walkthrough: An ugg boot is a sheepskin boot with the fleece inside, originally from Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The sheepskin boot has a fleecy lining, so it is a piece of fur-lined footwear, gear for cold feet.

clue.text: Shakespeare's fools steal Caesar's heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: to snipe is informally to pinch or steal
the fourth of the seven letters in Caesar's

explanation.surface: The Bard's clowns make off with Julius Caesar's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago in Othello calls Roderigo a snipe, a dupe, so the word is Shakespeare's for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A snipe, in Shakespeare's usage, is a simpleton or gull, so the plural names his kind of fools.

clue.text: Pike's relative swallowed fresh water – Jones remembered it

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the following word is made new by reordering
a fish that swallows something holds it inside its body

blocks.note: the gar, or garfish, is a long-snouted fish related to the pike
the five letters of water reordered

explanation.surface: A predatory fish gulped down some clean water, and a man named Jones recalled it.
explanation.walkthrough: Jones is David Jones, the Welsh poet whose 'In Parenthesis' recalls his service in the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: David Jones fought in the 1914 to 1918 conflict and wrote about it from memory, so it is the war he remembered.

clue.text: Sound pitched by Italy's sentimental songwriter

indicators.note: a sound is something heard, so the next word counts by how it is said

blocks.note: pitched means thrown
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: The music thrown out by an Italian writer of soppy songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Francesco Paolo Tosti wrote popular parlour songs such as 'Goodbye' around 1900.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosti was an Italian composer of drawing-room ballads, much loved for their tender, sugary feeling.

clue.text: The colourful work that scandalized some late Victorians

definitions.text: The colourful work that scandalized some late Victorians

blocks.note: surface reading: a vivid painting or brightly coloured artwork
setter's reading: the 1890s quarterly, named for a colour, linked with Beardsley and decadence

explanation.surface: A vividly coloured piece shocked some people in the 1890s.
explanation.walkthrough: The quarterly took its name and cover colour from the yellow-backed French novels thought racy; Beardsley was its art editor.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1890s literary periodical, bound in a bright colour, outraged respectable readers with its decadent art and writing.

clue.text: Old-style big city novel's rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: novel as an adjective means fresh

explanation.surface: A book about a great metropolis in an old-fashioned style has been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' is not a book here but an adjective. William Cobbett called London 'the Great Wen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobbett's dated term likens a swollen city to a growth on the skin, so it is an old name for a sprawling metropolis.

clue.text: A noble prisoner or depressed earl

blocks.note: feeling low
E is an abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: An aristocrat in jail, or perhaps just a gloomy lord.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marquis de Sade spent much of his life imprisoned, in the Bastille and elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The marquis was a nobleman who wrote many of his works while locked up, so he is a titled captive.

clue.text: American Getz's arrangement included two versions of one note that's long and flowing

definitions.note: adjectives describing the river rather than a noun for it

indicators.note: an arrangement in music reworks a piece, so the saxophonist's name is reworked
one thing that has another included holds it within itself

blocks.note: slang for a person from the USA
the jazz saxophonist's surname reordered
the Roman numeral I and the article an, both meaning one
a musical note

explanation.surface: Stan Getz's arrangement holds a sustained, legato note.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the old spelling of the Yangtze, China's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Chinese river is famously long and flows across the country, so the description fits it.
